q: In tennis, what word is used for a score of zero?
note: One popular explanation traces it to the French for egg, l'oeuf, after the shape of a nought on the scoreboard.

q: How many holes make up a full round of golf?
note: St Andrews settled on eighteen in 1764 and the rest of the golfing world simply copied it.

q: What is the feathered projectile hit back and forth in badminton called?
note: A traditional shuttlecock uses sixteen goose feathers, all taken from the same wing so it spins true.

q: In motor racing, which flag is waved as the winner crosses the finish line?
note: Its origins are murky, but the black and white squares have been ending American races since the early 1900s.

q: In a relay race, what is the object handed from one runner to the next?
note: Dropping it is bad enough, but handing it over outside the marked zone disqualifies the whole team.

q: In boxing, a referee counts to what number over a floored fighter to complete a knockout?
note: A referee can also give a standing eight count, pausing the bout to check whether a dazed fighter can continue.

q: In tennis, what term describes a game score of forty all?
note: From there a player must win two points in a row, and the word is thought to come from the French for two.

q: In golf, what is a score of one stroke under par on a hole called?
note: Two under is an eagle and three under an albatross, so the birds get grander as the scores get better.

q: In cricket, how many balls are bowled in an over?
note: Australia experimented with eight-ball overs for decades before finally falling into line in the late 1970s.

q: Which cycling race dresses its overall leader in a yellow jersey?
note: The jersey is yellow because the newspaper that founded the race was printed on yellow paper.

q: In volleyball, how many times may a team touch the ball before it must go back over the net?
note: The classic sequence has a name for each touch: the dig, the set and the spike.

q: In rugby, what is the name of the score awarded for grounding the ball behind the opponents' goal line?
note: It is called a try because it originally scored nothing at all, and merely earned a try at kicking a goal.

q: Which of the four tennis Grand Slam tournaments is played on grass?
note: The French Open is played on clay, while the Australian and US Opens use hard courts.

q: In gymnastics, what is the name of the narrow raised apparatus about four inches wide?
note: It is five metres long and stands over a metre off the floor, which is quite far enough to fall.

q: Which athletics event involves pushing a heavy metal ball from the shoulder as far as possible?
note: The men's shot weighs sixteen pounds, and throwing rather than pushing it is a foul.

q: In alpine skiing, what is the name of the event in which racers weave between closely set poles?
note: The word was borrowed from Norwegian, where it roughly means sloping track.

q: Which stroke is swum first in an individual medley race?
note: The order then runs backstroke, breaststroke and freestyle, so swimmers begin with the most punishing stroke.

q: In cricket, what is the term for a batter being dismissed without scoring a single run?
note: Going out to the very first ball you face is a golden duck, and failing to score in both innings is a pair.

q: In rowing, what is the title of the crew member who steers the boat and calls the rhythm?
note: The cox is the only one facing forwards, since the rowers travel backwards the entire way.

q: In modern competitive table tennis, a game is won by the first player to reach how many points?
note: Games ran to twenty-one until 2001, when the shorter format was brought in to make matches better television.
